plan.topic: Does tirzepatide lower blood pressure? SURMOUNT-1 blood pressure results plus the pooled meta-regression of 32 Phase 3 obesity-drug trials, reused from the verified, published 10-26 Short
plan.angle: Minimum-effort carousel built only from the verified 10-26 blood pressure Short script, with no new research. Drop it if that script isn't confirmed as verified. Slides: (1) the question; (2) SURMOUNT-1 systolic change, tirzepatide vs placebo, exactly as verified (adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, 72 weeks); (3) the pooled analysis: blood pressure fell more where weight fell more (about 0.34 mmHg per 1% of weight lost), labelled 'linked to · pooled data · not head-to-head · BP not the main goal'; (4) 'Never change your blood pressure medicines on your own; review lower readings with your doctor'; (5) common GI side effects; (6) 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line. No emoji.

social.instagram_caption:
Lower home BP readings on tirzepatide? Here's what one big trial in adults without diabetes found.

Average systolic (top) blood pressure fell 7.2 mmHg on tirzepatide (all doses pooled, counting everyone who started) vs 1.0 mmHg on placebo, over 72 weeks. Starting average was about 123 mmHg. This was a secondary measure, not the trial's main goal.

Weight loss may play a part: older diet-and-exercise trials have linked roughly 1 mmHg lower blood pressure per kg lost. That's a general link, not proof of how tirzepatide specifically works.

Keep your BP medicines as prescribed and don't change them on your own.

Save this for your next doctor's appointment, and bring a log of your home readings. Share this with someone who tracks their BP.

#Tirzepatide #BloodPressure #SURMOUNT1 #GLP1 #MetabolicHealth #Obesity

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

If you're on tirzepatide and your blood pressure readings have crept down, here's what the big trial actually found.

In the SURMOUNT-1 trial (adults without diabetes), average systolic blood pressure dropped 7.2 mmHg on tirzepatide (all doses pooled, counting everyone who started) vs 1.0 mmHg on placebo over 72 weeks, starting from an average of about 123 mmHg. It was a secondary measure, not the main goal of the study. Older diet-and-exercise trials have linked weight loss to lower blood pressure, but that's a general link, not a proven mechanism for this medicine specifically.

The practical takeaway: keep your blood pressure medicines as prescribed, log your readings, and bring them to your doctor rather than adjusting anything on your own.

Save this for your next appointment.

factcheck.summary:
This carousel is accurate and safe, so it passes. I checked these numbers against the sources and they match:
- **SURMOUNT-1 trial (PubMed abstract):** 2,539 adults without diabetes over 72 weeks. Average weight change was −15.0%, −19.5% and −20.9% on the three tirzepatide doses versus −3.1% on placebo. Side effects were mostly mild to moderate and came mainly while the dose was being increased.
- **Neter 2003 meta-analysis:** 25 randomized trials, 4,874 participants, about −1.05 mmHg systolic per kg lost. The weight loss came from eating less, exercise or both.
- **Krumholz 2024 (Heart):** a post hoc analysis of SURMOUNT-1. Average starting systolic blood pressure was 123.3 mmHg.

The stomach side-effect rates match the SURMOUNT-1 paper: nausea 24.6–33.3% vs 9.5%, diarrhea 18.7–22.7% vs 7.3%, constipation 11.7–17.1% vs 5.8%, vomiting 8.3–12.2% vs 1.7%.

**One number I couldn't confirm from a source.** The pooled −7.2 vs −1.0 mmHg systolic change counts everyone who started. It matches what I remember from the NEJM paper, but the NEJM page blocked access (403). The Krumholz figures (−8.1 vs −1.3 mmHg, a difference of −6.8) back up the direction and size of the effect. They come from a different way of counting people, so the carousel is right not to mix them in.

Safety framing is good. It says to keep blood pressure medicines as prescribed, flags dizziness and light-headedness, and includes the "don't change on your own" line, the "Not personal advice" line and the prescriber line. Five small fixes are listed below.

issues.problem: With the sound off, the pill shows the tirzepatide figure without the placebo comparison or the timeframe.
issues.fix: Change stat to: "-7.2 vs -1.0 mmHg" and headline to: "Tirzepatide (all doses) vs placebo: average change in systolic (top) blood pressure, 72 weeks"

issues.claim: average starting systolic BP was about 123 mmHg, so most did not have high blood pressure
issues.problem: An average can't tell you how many people had high blood pressure, so 'most did not' goes further than the source shows.
issues.fix: Replace with: "Adults without diabetes; average starting systolic BP was about 123 mmHg."

issues.problem: This is a bit too broad. A SURMOUNT-1 post hoc analysis did look at blood pressure with tirzepatide. What wasn't tested with tirzepatide is the 1 mmHg-per-kg rule.
issues.fix: Label: "The per-kg rule is from older trials"; detail: "Diet and exercise trials, not GLP-1 medicines"

issues.claim: tirzepatide was linked to lower blood pressure on average
issues.problem: SURMOUNT-1 was a randomized trial, so 'compared with placebo' is the accurate wording, and it gives the comparison too. 'Linked to' undersells it. Not misleading, just imprecise.
issues.fix: "In SURMOUNT-1 (adults without diabetes), blood pressure fell more on tirzepatide than on placebo, on average. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you."

issues.problem: The URL returns 403. The house rule is no 403 links in the source list.
issues.fix: Use https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35658024/ (Jastreboff AM et al., N Engl J Med 2022;387:205-216).
